newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria prepares currency board regime.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria prepares currency board regime.

text.p: Bulgaria's government and central bank have approved an International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposal for a strict monetary regime to stabilise the economy and halt the fall in the lev, but final details still need to be worked out and approved by parliament.
A currency board system is expected to be introduced early next year for an indefinite period.

It will require that levs in circulation and commercial banks' mimimum reserves at the central bank match central bank foreign exchange and gold reserves, effectively pegging the lev to the dollar or the mark at a fixed exchange rate.
Currency boards have been used to repair crumbling financial systems and curb inflation in other countries such as Argentina, Lithuania and Estonia.
According to the IMF, the system virtually bans domestic money creation and prevents the central bank from directly financing the government's budget deficit.
The interbank market would continue to operate, possibly with limits set for the lev to fluctuate on either side of the pegged rate, some analysts said.
But key issues that still need to be determined include to which currency and at what rate the lev will be pegged and how restrictive the system will be.
The U.S. dollar is widely perceived as a benchmark of stability and most people convert savings into dollars. Germany, however, is Bulgaria's biggest investor and trade partner.

Neither the IMF nor the government has said what exchange rate would be sought for the lev under the currency board. Officials say the rate has yet to be discussed with IMF technical experts and would depend on the level of financial support provided by the IMF and other lenders.
Some economists said the IMF was unlikely to support introducing a board at a very devalued lev rate as this could increase inflation.
Dealers in Sofia speculated the rate would be close to the current level of about 350 levs to the dollar.

At the end of October, central bank reserves were $541 million, gold reserves were worth about $400 million and levs in circulation and commercial banks' minumum reserve deposits at the central bank total 180 billion levs ($518 million).
The government has been trying to seek financial help from the IMF and European Union, but it is unclear if these efforts will be successful.
Critics of the plan said the currency board does not address the problem of Bulgaria's domestic debt, which reached 668 billion levs at the end of October.
But the IMF says the currency board will lead to a fall in inflation and interest rates, now at about 180 percent, which would cut borrowing costs.

The IMF proposed rolling over maturity payments in the short term, but finance ministry officials doubted financial institutions struggling to operate under the austere currency board system would be able to buy government securities at all.
Some economists also said a currency board could lead to more closures of illiquid banks because it would halt commercial bank refinancing.
But the IMF said the markets for government securities would continue to function normally.

"In fact, the stability of financial markets under a currency board would likely result in an increase in confidence in the securities market," said a statement from the IMF resident mission in Sofia.

Other economists said commercial bank refinancing would also depend on what type of currency board is adopted. Under a softer approach, the central bank's banking supervision department would still be able to provide limited refinancing to commercial banks, they said.
